old.quote: Input real floating-point x_1,...,x_n, n>=1. Set d=ceil(log_2 n), append 2^d-n exact zero leaves, and round the sum at each internal node of the balanced tree. An unmatched leaf may be copied. If a rounded node fails the operationwise range rule, return range-failure and its tree index; otherwise return the root s-hat. This finite tree terminates after 2^d-1 additions; accuracy is asserted only on success.

Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ with $n\ge 1$, let $u\ge 0$, let
$\delta_0,\dots,\delta_{n-1}\in\mathbb{R}$ satisfy $|\delta_i|\le u$ for every
$i<n$, and suppose $n u<1$. Then

$$\prod_{i<n}(1+\delta_i)=1+\theta_n\qquad\text{with}\qquad|\theta_n|\le\gamma_n:=\frac{n u}{1-n u}.$$

new.quote:
Input real floating-point values $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, $n\ge1$. Set $d=\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$, place these values in leaves $1,\ldots,n$ from left to right, and append $2^d-n$ exact zero leaves. At level $\ell=1,\ldots,d$, replace each consecutive pair of current nodes $(a_{\ell-1,2j-1},a_{\ell-1,2j})$, in increasing $j=1,\ldots,2^{d-\ell}$, by
$$a_{\ell,j}=\operatorname{fl}(a_{\ell-1,2j-1}+a_{\ell-1,2j}).$$
If an operation fails, return `range-failure` with the first failing level $\ell$ and node $j$ in this level-by-level, left-to-right order. For $d=0$, return $x_1$ with no additions. Otherwise return the single node $a_{d,1}$. The tree is fully specified, terminates after $2^d-1$ additions, and its accuracy is asserted only on success.

Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ with $n\ge 1$, let $u\ge 0$, let
$\delta_0,\dots,\delta_{n-1}\in\mathbb{R}$ satisfy $|\delta_i|\le u$ for every
$i<n$, and suppose $n u<1$. Then

$$\prod_{i<n}(1+\delta_i)=1+\theta_n\qquad\text{with}\qquad|\theta_n|\le\gamma_n:=\frac{n u}{1-n u}.$$

old.claim: For Kahan write y_i=x_i-c_{i-1}+epsilon_i^y and s_i=s_{i-1}+y_i+epsilon_i^s. Then d_i=s_i-s_{i-1}+epsilon_i^d and c_i=d_i-y_i+epsilon_i^c=epsilon_i^s+epsilon_i^d+epsilon_i^c.

In either Neumaier branch exact algebra gives t_i+a_i=s_{i-1}+x_i+epsilon_i^t+epsilon_i^q+epsilon_i^a: substitute q_i=s_{i-1}-t_i in the first branch or q_i=x_i-t_i in the second, including their signed rounding errors. The compensation update adds epsilon_i^c. Summing s_i+c_i-(s_{i-1}+c_{i-1}) telescopes, and the final rounded return adds epsilon^f.

Summing s_i-s_{i-1}=x_i-c_{i-1}+epsilon_i^y+epsilon_i^s and substituting the formula for c_{i-1} cancels epsilon_i^s for i<n and gives the displayed Kahan identity. Bounding the remaining local errors by [F3] yields its stated finite bound.

Taking absolute values and applying [F3] gives exactly uP_i for the four executed operations in iteration i; the final operation contributes u|s_n+c_n|. This proves the displayed Neumaier bound. No step divides by the exact sum, so no uniform relative bound follows.

new.claim: For Kahan write y_i=x_i-c_{i-1}+epsilon_i^y and s_i=s_{i-1}+y_i+epsilon_i^s. Then d_i=s_i-s_{i-1}+epsilon_i^d and c_i=d_i-y_i+epsilon_i^c=epsilon_i^s+epsilon_i^d+epsilon_i^c.

In the first Neumaier branch, q_i=s_{i-1}-t_i+epsilon_i^q and a_i=q_i+x_i+epsilon_i^a, so t_i+a_i=s_{i-1}+x_i+epsilon_i^q+epsilon_i^a. In the second branch, q_i=x_i-t_i+epsilon_i^q and a_i=q_i+s_{i-1}+epsilon_i^a give the same identity. Thus the error in forming t_i cancels in both branches. Since s_i=t_i and c_i=c_{i-1}+a_i+epsilon_i^c, summing s_i+c_i-(s_{i-1}+c_{i-1}) telescopes to the corrected Neumaier identity before final rounding; the returned addition contributes epsilon^f.

Summing s_i-s_{i-1}=x_i-c_{i-1}+epsilon_i^y+epsilon_i^s and substituting the formula for c_{i-1} cancels epsilon_i^s for i<n and gives the displayed Kahan identity. Bounding the remaining local errors by [F3] yields its stated finite bound.

Take absolute values in the corrected identity. By [F3], the q_i error is bounded by u times the sum of the magnitudes in the first branch-specific term of P_i, the a_i error by u times the second branch-specific term, and the c_i error by u(|c_{i-1}|+|a_i|). Their sum is at most uP_i because the remaining term u(|s_{i-1}|+|x_i|) is nonnegative. The final addition contributes at most u|s_n+c_n|. This proves the unchanged conservative Neumaier bound. No step divides by the exact sum, so no uniform relative bound follows.

old.quote: Input a Hermitian positive-definite matrix $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, whose real and imaginary components are in the floating-point system, in the convention of [[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]]; real matrices are included. Set L-hat=0. For j=1,...,n, form the diagonal sum from rounded real squares of the real and imaginary components of l_jk and rounded additions, then p_j=fl(a_jj-sum_{k<j}|l_jk|^2). If an operation fails or p_j is not positive normal, return failure(j). Set l_jj=fl(sqrt(p_j)); unless this is positive normal return failure(j). For i>j, form c_ij by sequential complex products with six real operations each and componentwise rounded additions; form r_ij=fl(a_ij-c_ij) componentwise and divide each real component by positive l_jj with one rounded real division. Any range failure returns failure(j) with the operation index. If all columns finish, return success(L-hat). The loops are finite. By [[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]], exact positive definiteness ensures an exact factor exists, but does not ensure the rounded algorithm succeeds.

Let $n\ge 1$ and let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, with the real case obtained by
restricting scalars to $\mathbb R$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $A$ has a Cholesky factorisation $A=LL^*$ with $L$ lower triangular and
   positive real diagonal.
2. $A$ is Hermitian positive definite.

When these conditions hold, the factor $L$ is unique.

Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ with $n\ge 1$, let $u\ge 0$, let
$\delta_0,\dots,\delta_{n-1}\in\mathbb{R}$ satisfy $|\delta_i|\le u$ for every
$i<n$, and suppose $n u<1$. Then

$$\prod_{i<n}(1+\delta_i)=1+\theta_n\qquad\text{with}\qquad|\theta_n|\le\gamma_n:=\frac{n u}{1-n u}.$$

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

new.quote:
Input a Hermitian positive-definite matrix $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, whose real and imaginary components are in the floating-point system, using the convention of [[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]]; real matrices are included. Initialize every entry of $\widehat L$ to zero. Process columns $j=1,\ldots,n$ in increasing order. For the diagonal, initialize $s=0$ and, for $k=1,\ldots,j-1$ in increasing order, compute
$$r_k=\operatorname{fl}(\Re(\widehat l_{jk})^2),\quad t_k=\operatorname{fl}(\Im(\widehat l_{jk})^2),\quad q_k=\operatorname{fl}(r_k+t_k),\quad s=\operatorname{fl}(s+q_k),$$
in that order. Then compute $p_j=\operatorname{fl}(a_{jj}-s)$. If an operation fails, or if $p_j$ is not positive and normal, return `failure` with pivot $j$ and the first failing operation location. Otherwise compute $\widehat l_{jj}=\operatorname{fl}(\sqrt{p_j})$; if it is not positive and normal, return `failure` at pivot $j$.

For each $i=j+1,\ldots,n$ in increasing order, initialize the complex accumulator $c_{ij}=0$. For $k=1,\ldots,j-1$ in increasing order, compute the complex product $w_{ik}=\widehat l_{ik}\overline{\widehat l_{jk}}$ using exactly the six real operations of the complex-product convention in [[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]], then update
$$\Re(c_{ij})\gets\operatorname{fl}(\Re(c_{ij})+\Re(w_{ik})),\qquad \Im(c_{ij})\gets\operatorname{fl}(\Im(c_{ij})+\Im(w_{ik})).$$
After this dot product, compute $r_{ij}=a_{ij}-c_{ij}$ by one rounded real subtraction for each component, then compute each component of $\widehat l_{ij}=r_{ij}/\widehat l_{jj}$ by one rounded real division. The empty dot product is zero. On any failure return `failure` with pivot $j$ and its first failing operation location (stage, column, row, inner index, component, and operation where applicable), with the diagonal and row loops ordered as stated. If all columns finish, return `success(\widehat L)`. All loops are finite. By [[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]], exact positive definiteness ensures an exact factor exists, but does not ensure the rounded algorithm succeeds.

old.claim: If $x=0$, the algorithm copies $B$ and the zero column; take $H=I$ and $E=0$. Otherwise put $N=\|x\|_2$, $\alpha_0=-\sigma N$, $v_0=x-\alpha_0e_1$ and $V_0=\|v_0\|_2\ge N$. The nonnegative scaled squared-norm sum has each exact squared input multiplied by at most $r+2$ factors $1+\delta$, $|\delta|\le u$: two from scaling and at most $r$ from squaring and subsequent additions. Thus the computed norm divided by $N$ lies between $(1-u)^{r/2+3}$ and $(1+u)^{r/2+3}$ after square root and rescaling. For exponent $p\ge1$, convexity of $t^p$ on $t>0$ gives $1-(1-u)^p\le(1+u)^p-1$. Hence $|\widehat\alpha-\alpha_0|\le e_rN$. Only the first stored coordinate can differ from $v_0$, and subtraction gives $\|v-v_0\|_2\le(e_r+u(2+e_r))N=d_rN$. Success gives nonzero stored $v$.

For nonzero vectors $a,b$, adding and subtracting $a/\|b\|$ and using the reverse triangle inequality gives $\|a/\|a\|-b/\|b\|\|\le2\|a-b\|/\|b\|$. For unit $z,w$, expanding $zz^T-ww^T=(z-w)z^T+w(z-w)^T$ gives norm at most $2\|z-w\|$. Consequently $\|H(v)-H(v_0)\|_2\le8\|v-v_0\|/V_0\le8d_r$. Since $H(v_0)x=\alpha_0e_1$, the overwritten column differs from $H(v)x$ by at most $(e_r+8d_r)N$.

Put $V=\|v\|_2$. The rounded positive dot product satisfies $(1-u)^r V^2\le w\le(1+u)^r V^2$ by expansion of its products and additions, including exact zeros. The division defining $\widehat\tau$ therefore gives $|\widehat\tau V^2/2-1|\le a_r$; the upper deviation dominates the lower by multiplying the positive denominators. A sequential signed dot product differs from its exact value by at most $g_r\sum_i|v_iB_{ij}|\le g_rV\|B_{:j}\|_2$, by the same factor expansion and [F4].

The exact rank-one update has norm at most $2\|B\|_F$. Replacing its coefficient by $\widehat\tau$, its dot by the computed dot, and its two multiplications by rounded multiplications bounds the update error by $c_r\|B\|_F$: successively the nonnegative majorants multiply by $1+a_r$, $1+g_r$, and $(1+u)^2$, then subtract the exact majorant $2$. Final subtraction adds at most $u(\|B\|_F+\|U\|_F)\le u(3+c_r)\|B\|_F$. Thus $\|\widehat B-H(v)B\|_F\le((1+u)c_r+3u)\|B\|_F$. The same computation applies to any separate block $Y$.

The first-column and remaining-column errors occupy disjoint columns, so their squared Frobenius norms add. Steps 1.2 and 2.2 give $\|C_+-H(v)C\|_F\le\kappa_r\|C\|_F$. Choose $E=H(v)C_+-C$; orthogonality gives the claimed equation and equal error norm. Each displayed coefficient increases with $r$ and has zero constant term and finite first derivative at $u=0$, proving the stated asymptotics.

old.quote: Input a real active column $x\in\mathbb F^r$ and trailing block $B\in\mathbb F^{r\times q}$, with entries in the floating-point system, $r\ge1$, and $q\ge0$. If $x=0$, return the identity action and copy $B$. Otherwise let $s=\max_i|x_i|>0$, compute $z_i=\operatorname{fl}(x_i/s)$ and $t=\operatorname{fl}(\sum_i z_i^2)$ by sequential rounded operations, then $\widehat r=\operatorname{fl}(s\operatorname{fl}(\sqrt t))$. Set $\sigma=1$ when $x_1=0$ and $\sigma=\operatorname{sign}(x_1)$ otherwise, $\widehat\alpha=-\sigma\widehat r$, $v_i=\operatorname{fl}(x_i-\widehat\alpha\,1_{i=1})$, $w=\operatorname{fl}(v^Tv)$, and $\widehat\tau=\operatorname{fl}(2/w)$. Compute $d=\operatorname{fl}(v^TB)$ by sequential rounded products and additions, $p_i=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\tau v_i)$, $U_{ij}=\operatorname{fl}(p_i d_j)$, and $\widehat B_{ij}=\operatorname{fl}(B_{ij}-U_{ij})$. The complete active output is $C_+=[\widehat\alpha e_1\;\widehat B]$: write exact zeros below its first diagonal entry. This fixes the multiplication order and includes the column overwrite in the analyzed step. Return the first range failure on any invalid or out-of-range operation; return failure if $t$, $\widehat r$, or $w$ is not positive normal, or any intermediate is nonfinite. Otherwise return $(v,\widehat\tau,\widehat\alpha,C_+)$. Store these reflectors to represent the exact orthogonal product; a rounded explicit dense product is a separate output with its own arithmetic error. The exact reflector associated with nonzero stored $v$ is $H(v)=I-2vv^T/(v^Tv)$, using [[def-householder-reflector]] and the QR convention of [[def-full-reduced-and-column-pivoted-computational-qr-factorisations]]. This definition does not assert a local backward-error bound.

Let the representable set, normal range, and unit roundoff be as in [[def-standard-relative-floating-point-model-and-unit-roundoff]]. Here fl is round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, on each real exact result that is zero or normal; every other nonzero exact result (subnormal or overflow), NaN, infinity, invalid operation, or division by zero returns range-failure. A real add, subtract, multiply, or divide is one rounded operation. For positive in-range x, fl(sqrt(x)) is correctly rounded to nearest, ties-to-even, and fails unless its result is positive and normal. A real fused multiply-add returns the correctly rounded value of the single exact expression ab+c; it is not two operations.

Complex addition and subtraction round real and imaginary components separately. A complex product (a+ib)(c+id) uses four rounded real products ac, bd, ad, bc, then rounded subtraction and addition, for six real operations. Conjugation and sign changes are exact. Scaling and division by a positive real scalar round each complex component separately; no other complex division primitive is used here.

A procedure succeeds only when each exact intermediate is zero or normal and every rounded output is finite; otherwise it returns the first range-failure with its operation or pivot index. For ku<1 write gamma_k=ku/(1-ku). This is a no-underflow success model, not the gradual-underflow model.

Let $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$.

1. Every Householder reflector $H_v=I-2vv^*$ is orthogonal or unitary.
2. For every nonzero $z\in \mathbb F^m$, there is a Householder reflector $H$

Input a real active column $x\in\mathbb F^r$ and trailing block $B\in\mathbb F^{r\times q}$ with entries in the floating-point system, $r\ge1$, $q\ge0$. If every component of $x$ is zero, return the identity action and a copy of $B$, with the active output column set to exact zeros, so that $C_+=[0e_1\;B]$; return $(v=0,\widehat\tau=0,\widehat\alpha=0,C_+)$ marked `identity`. Otherwise compute $s=\max_{1\le i\le r}|x_i|>0$, and then, in increasing $i$, compute $z_i=\operatorname{fl}(x_i/s)$. Initialize $t=0$ and, in increasing $i$, compute $a_i=\operatorname{fl}(z_i z_i)$ followed by $t=\operatorname{fl}(t+a_i)$. Compute $h=\operatorname{fl}(\sqrt t)$ and then $\widehat r=\operatorname{fl}(s h)$. Set $\sigma=1$ if $x_1=0$ and $\sigma=\operatorname{sign}(x_1)$ otherwise, and set $\widehat\alpha=-\sigma\widehat r$ using the exact sign change. Compute $v_1=\operatorname{fl}(x_1-\widehat\alpha)$, then copy $v_i=x_i$ exactly for $i=2,\ldots,r$.

Initialize $w=0$ and, in increasing $i$, compute $a_i=\operatorname{fl}(v_i v_i)$ followed by $w=\operatorname{fl}(w+a_i)$. Then compute $\widehat\tau=\operatorname{fl}(2/w)$. For each column $j=1,\ldots,q$ in increasing order, initialize $d_j=0$ and, in increasing $i$, compute $a_{ij}=\operatorname{fl}(v_i B_{ij})$ followed by $d_j=\operatorname{fl}(d_j+a_{ij})$. After all $d_j$ have been computed, in increasing $i$ compute $p_i=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\tau v_i)$. Then, in increasing $j$ and within each column in increasing $i$, compute $U_{ij}=\operatorname{fl}(p_i d_j)$ and $\widehat B_{ij}=\operatorname{fl}(B_{ij}-U_{ij})$ in that order. The complete active output is $C_+=[\widehat\alpha e_1\;\widehat B]$, with exact zeros written below its first diagonal entry. If any elementary operation fails, return the first range failure with its stage and indices in the order above. Also return failure if $t$, $\widehat r$, or $w$ is not positive normal, or any intermediate is nonfinite. Otherwise return $(v,\widehat\tau,\widehat\alpha,C_+)$ marked `reflector`. For a separate block $Y$, apply the stored reflector by computing its sequential column dots in increasing column order, then the vector $p_i=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\tau v_i)$ in increasing $i$, and then each rounded product and subtraction by increasing column and row; omit the target-column overwrite. Store reflector factors with their identity/reflector marker to represent the exact orthogonal product; a rounded explicit dense product is a separate output with its own arithmetic error. For a nonzero stored $v$, the associated exact reflector is $H(v)=I-2vv^T/(v^Tv)$, using [[def-householder-reflector]] and the QR convention of [[def-full-reduced-and-column-pivoted-computational-qr-factorisations]]. This definition does not assert a local backward-error bound.

Let the representable set, normal range, and unit roundoff be as in [[def-standard-relative-floating-point-model-and-unit-roundoff]]. Here fl is round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, on each real exact result that is zero or normal; every other nonzero exact result (subnormal or overflow), NaN, infinity, invalid operation, or division by zero returns range-failure. A real add, subtract, multiply, or divide is one rounded operation. For positive in-range x, fl(sqrt(x)) is correctly rounded to nearest, ties-to-even, and fails unless its result is positive and normal. A real fused multiply-add returns the correctly rounded value of the single exact expression ab+c; it is not two operations.

Complex addition and subtraction round real and imaginary components separately. A complex product (a+ib)(c+id) uses four rounded real products ac, bd, ad, bc, then rounded subtraction and addition, for six real operations. Conjugation and sign changes are exact. Scaling and division by a positive real scalar round each complex component separately; no other complex division primitive is used here.

A procedure succeeds only when each exact intermediate is zero or normal and every rounded output is finite; otherwise it returns the first range-failure with its operation or pivot index. For ku<1 write gamma_k=ku/(1-ku). This is a no-underflow success model, not the gradual-underflow model.

$i<n$, and suppose $n u<1$. Then

$$\prod_{i<n}(1+\delta_i)=1+\theta_n\qquad\text{with}\qquad|\theta_n|\le\gamma_n:=\frac{n u}{1-n u}.$$

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Input nonsingular real $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, and $b,x_0\in\mathbb R^n$, nonsingular factor matrix $\widehat A$ formed at factorization precision $u_f$, residual precision $u_r$, solve/update precision $u_w$, finite budget $N\ge0$, tolerance $\tau\ge0$, certified nonnegative constants $\eta_r,\xi_r,\eta_w,\xi_w$, and a certified contraction upper bound $0\le q_{\mathrm{cert}}<1$. Let $x_*=A^{-1}b$ be the unique exact solution. Use the operationwise model of [[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]] separately at $u_f,u_r,u_w$. The exact data $A,b$ are available to residual evaluation at $u_r$; stored iterates and correction updates use $u_w$. At iteration $k$, compute $\widehat r_k=\operatorname{fl}_{u_r}(b-Ax_k)$, solve for a correction using the supplied triangular factors of $\widehat A$ and the recurrence in [[def-forward-and-back-substitution-for-triangular-systems]], then round $x_{k+1}=\operatorname{fl}_{u_w}(x_k+\widehat z_k)$. A certificate must bound the residual defect $\widehat r_k=A(x_*-x_k)+\delta_{r,k}$ by $\|\delta_{r,k}\|_2\le\eta_r(\|A\|_2\|x_k\|_2+\|b\|_2)+\xi_r$, and the combined solve/update residual-equivalent error is defined by
$$x_{k+1}=x_k+\widehat A^{-1}(\widehat r_k+\delta_{w,k}),\qquad \|\delta_{w,k}\|_2\le\eta_w\|\widehat r_k\|_2+\xi_w.$$
The certificate must verify that $q\le q_{\mathrm{cert}}$, where
$$q=\|I-\widehat A^{-1}A\|_2+ \|\widehat A^{-1}\|_2((1+\eta_w)\eta_r+\eta_w)\|A\|_2.$$
If a required range or nonsingularity check fails, a certificate is unavailable, or $q\le q_{\mathrm{cert}}<1$ is not certified, return inconclusive. Otherwise test the current residual, return residual-tolerance if its computed norm is at most $\tau$, and update at most $N$ times; return budget-exhausted after $N$ unsuccessful updates. Return the current iterate with its status. The procedure is finite and does not claim exact termination or unconditional convergence.

Let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$ and let $m,n,q\in\mathbb{N}$, with the
induced $p$-norms of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

1. **Compatibility.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and every
   $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert Ax\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert x\rVert_p.$$
2. **Submultiplicativity.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and
   $B\in M_{n\times q}(\mathbb{R})$,
   $$\lVert AB\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert B\rVert_p.$$
3. **Normalisation.** For every $n\ge 1$,
   $$\lVert I_n\rVert_p=1,$$
   where $I_n$ is the identity matrix of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]];
   at $n=0$ the unique empty matrix $I_0\in M_0(\mathbb{R})$ has
   $\lVert I_0\rVert_p=0$, the convention of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

Input nonsingular real $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, exact data $b\in\mathbb R^n$, and an initial iterate $x_0$ stored at solve/update precision $u_w$. Also input stored triangular factors $\widehat L,\widehat U$ formed at factorization precision $u_f$, where $\widehat L$ is lower triangular, $\widehat U$ is upper triangular, both have nonzero diagonals, and $\widehat A:=\widehat L\widehat U$ is the exact real product; thus $\widehat A$ is nonsingular. Input residual precision $u_r$, solve/update precision $u_w$, finite update budget $N\ge0$, tolerance $\tau\ge0$, a stagnation window $K_{\rm stag}\ge1$, certified nonnegative constants $\eta_r,\xi_r,\eta_w,\xi_w$, and a certified contraction upper bound $0\le q_{\rm cert}<1$. Let $x_*=A^{-1}b$. Use the operationwise model of [[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]] at each stated precision. Entries of the exact data $A,b$ are available as real operands to the residual operations; the stored factors, iterates, residuals, and corrections are used as their exact represented values in those operations.

Before iterating, check the factor conditions and a supplied certificate establishing $q\le q_{\rm cert}<1$, where
$$q=\|I-\widehat A^{-1}A\|_2+\|\widehat A^{-1}\|_2\bigl((1+\eta_w)\eta_r+\eta_w\bigr)\|A\|_2.$$
The certificate must include certified norm bounds sufficient to verify this inequality; an unavailable or unverified certificate returns `inconclusive` with $x_0$.

Before entering the iteration loop, initialize the consecutive-equality counter $c_{\rm stag}=0$ and mark the preceding residual as undefined. Retain this counter and preceding residual across iterations; do not reinitialize them inside the loop. The counter records the number of consecutive equalities between adjacent successfully certified computed residual vectors.

For each $k=0,\ldots,N$, compute the residual by rows in increasing $i$: initialize $s_i=0$, then for $j=1,\ldots,n$ in increasing order compute $p_{ij}=\operatorname{fl}_{u_r}(A_{ij}x_{k,j})$ and $s_i=\operatorname{fl}_{u_r}(s_i+p_{ij})$; finally set $\widehat r_{k,i}=\operatorname{fl}_{u_r}(b_i-s_i)$. Any operationwise range failure returns `inconclusive` with the current iterate and the first failing row, column, and operation. Define the exact residual defect $\delta_{r,k}=\widehat r_k-(b-Ax_k)$, so $\widehat r_k=A(x_*-x_k)+\delta_{r,k}$. A supplied per-iteration certificate must establish
$$\|\delta_{r,k}\|_2\le\eta_r(\|A\|_2\|x_k\|_2+\|b\|_2)+\xi_r.$$
If it is unavailable or cannot be verified from certified norm bounds, return `inconclusive` with the current iterate.

Use the retained consecutive-equality counter and preceding residual. Use the exact Euclidean norm of the stored residual vector for the status comparison; this is a comparison of the already computed vector, not an additional rounded arithmetic operation. If $\|\widehat r_k\|_2\le\tau$, return `residual-tolerance` with $x_k$. If a preceding residual exists, compare its components exactly with those of $\widehat r_k$: if all are equal, increment $c_{\rm stag}$ by one; otherwise reset it to zero. If $c_{\rm stag}=K_{\rm stag}$, return `successful-stagnation` with $x_k$. This status certifies only that the last $K_{\rm stag}$ successful updates produced identical computed residual vectors, with all range and contraction certificates accepted; it certifies neither a small exact error nor convergence. Before any further update, store $\widehat r_k$ as the preceding residual.

If $k=N$ and neither status above was returned, return `budget-exhausted` with $x_k$. Otherwise solve $\widehat L y_k=\widehat r_k$ by forward substitution, then $\widehat U\widehat z_k=y_k$ by backward substitution, using precision $u_w$. For forward substitution, visit rows $i=1,\ldots,n$ in increasing order, initialize $s_i=0$, and for $j=1,\ldots,i-1$ in increasing order compute $p_{ij}=\operatorname{fl}_{u_w}(\widehat L_{ij}y_{k,j})$ and $s_i=\operatorname{fl}_{u_w}(s_i+p_{ij})$, then $t_i=\operatorname{fl}_{u_w}(\widehat r_{k,i}-s_i)$ and $y_{k,i}=\operatorname{fl}_{u_w}(t_i/\widehat L_{ii})$. For backward substitution, visit rows $i=n,\ldots,1$ in decreasing order, initialize $s_i=0$, and for $j=i+1,\ldots,n$ in increasing order compute $p_{ij}=\operatorname{fl}_{u_w}(\widehat U_{ij}\widehat z_{k,j})$ and $s_i=\operatorname{fl}_{u_w}(s_i+p_{ij})$, then $t_i=\operatorname{fl}_{u_w}(y_{k,i}-s_i)$ and $\widehat z_{k,i}=\operatorname{fl}_{u_w}(t_i/\widehat U_{ii})$. Update components in increasing order by $x_{k+1,i}=\operatorname{fl}_{u_w}(x_{k,i}+\widehat z_{k,i})$. A failed operation returns `inconclusive` with the current iterate and first failing operation location.

After a successful update, define the exact residual-equivalent update defect
$$\delta_{w,k}:=\widehat A(x_{k+1}-x_k)-\widehat r_k,$$
so $x_{k+1}=x_k+\widehat A^{-1}(\widehat r_k+\delta_{w,k})$. A supplied per-iteration certificate must establish $\|\delta_{w,k}\|_2\le\eta_w\|\widehat r_k\|_2+\xi_w$; if unavailable or unverified, return `inconclusive` with $x_{k+1}$. Continue until one of the stated statuses is returned. All loops are finite. The procedure does not claim exact termination or unconditional convergence.

The exact orthogonal product represented by the stored reflectors has reduced first $n$ columns $\widehat Q$, and the computed triangular block is $\widehat R$. Then
$$A+\Delta A=\widehat Q\widehat R,\qquad \|\Delta A\|_F\le\beta_Q\|A\|_F.$$
Applying the stored reflectors in the same order to a separate vector $b$, by their rounded rank-one updates without column overwrites, gives a full vector $\widehat c$ satisfying
$$\|\widehat c-Q_{\rm full}^Tb\|_2\le\beta_Q\|b\|_2.$$

Let $R\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be upper triangular with nonzero diagonal, $y\in\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge1$, and $(n+3)u<1$. Compute descending substitution by the sequential rounded dot $s_i=\operatorname{fl}(\sum_{j>i}R_{ij}\widehat x_j)$ (empty sum zero), $t_i=\operatorname{fl}(y_i-s_i)$, and $\widehat x_i=\operatorname{fl}(t_i/R_{ii})$. $$(R+\Delta R)\widehat x=y,\qquad |\Delta R|\le\gamma_{n+3}|R|,\qquad \|\Delta R\|_F\le\gamma_{n+3}\|R\|_F.$$
In particular $\widehat x=0$ forces $y=0$. Forward substitution has the transposed conclusion.

Let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb R)$ with $m\ge n\ge 1$ and full column rank.
Let

$$A=\widehat Q\widehat R$$

be a reduced QR factorisation, with
$$\widehat Q^{\mathsf T}\widehat Q=I_n$$

Input real floating-point x_1,...,x_n, n>=1. Set d=ceil(log_2 n), append 2^d-n exact zero leaves, and round the sum at each internal node of the balanced tree. An unmatched leaf may be copied. If a rounded node fails the operationwise range rule, return range-failure and its tree index; otherwise return the root s-hat. This finite tree terminates after 2^d-1 additions; accuracy is asserted only on success.

Input real floating-point values $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, $n\ge1$. Set $d=\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$, place these values in leaves $1,\ldots,n$ from left to right, and append $2^d-n$ exact zero leaves. At level $\ell=1,\ldots,d$, replace each consecutive pair of current nodes $(a_{\ell-1,2j-1},a_{\ell-1,2j})$, in increasing $j=1,\ldots,2^{d-\ell}$, by
$$a_{\ell,j}=\operatorname{fl}(a_{\ell-1,2j-1}+a_{\ell-1,2j}).$$
If an operation fails, return `range-failure` with the first failing level $\ell$ and node $j$ in this level-by-level, left-to-right order. For $d=0$, return $x_1$ with no additions. Otherwise return the single node $a_{d,1}$. The tree is fully specified, terminates after $2^d-1$ additions, and its accuracy is asserted only on success.

new.claim: The value 2^-53 is half an ulp at 1, so 1+2^-53 rounds to 1. Ordinary summation then returns 0.
Neumaier step 2 selects |s_1|>=|x_2| and gives t_2=1,q_2=0,a_2=2^-53,c_2=2^-53; step 3 gives t_3=0,q_3=1,a_3=0,c_3=2^-53.
The final exact addition 0+2^-53 is 2^-53, which is the exact sum; [F2] records this correction without claiming uniform relative accuracy.

old.quote: For real floating-point inputs $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ initialize s_0=c_0=0. Set t_i=fl(s_{i-1}+x_i). If |s_{i-1}|>=|x_i| set q_i=fl(s_{i-1}-t_i), a_i=fl(q_i+x_i); otherwise set q_i=fl(x_i-t_i), a_i=fl(q_i+s_{i-1}). Then set c_i=fl(c_{i-1}+a_i), s_i=t_i. Return fl(s_n+c_n), or the first range-failure and operation index. The branch test is defined for all real inputs and the loop terminates.

For successfully processed real inputs $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, let $\epsilon_i^y,\epsilon_i^s,\epsilon_i^d,\epsilon_i^c$ be the signed errors in the four Kahan operations. Then
$$s_n-\sum_{i=1}^n x_i=\sum_{i=1}^n\epsilon_i^y+\epsilon_n^s-\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}(\epsilon_i^d+\epsilon_i^c),$$
hence
$$|s_n-\sum_i x_i|\le u\sum_i|x_i-c_{i-1}|+u|s_{n-1}+y_n|+u\sum_{i<n}(|s_i-s_{i-1}|+|d_i-y_i|).$$
For Neumaier, let $\epsilon_i^t,\epsilon_i^q,\epsilon_i^a,\epsilon_i^c$ be the signed errors at the actually executed operations and $\epsilon^f$ the final rounding error. Then
$$\widehat s-\sum_i x_i=\sum_i(\epsilon_i^t+\epsilon_i^q+\epsilon_i^a+\epsilon_i^c)+\epsilon^f.$$
For each $i$, define $P_i$ by the branch-specific expression below. Then
$$|\widehat s-\sum_i x_i|\le u\sum_iP_i+u|s_n+c_n|,$$
where the final term accounts for the last rounded addition. These are finite data-dependent bounds, not uniform relative-error claims.

$$P_i=|s_{i-1}|+|x_i|+ \begin{cases}|s_{i-1}|+|t_i|,&|s_{i-1}|\ge|x_i|,\\|x_i|+|t_i|,&|s_{i-1}|<|x_i|\end{cases} +\begin{cases}|q_i|+|x_i|,&|s_{i-1}|\ge|x_i|,\\|q_i|+|s_{i-1}|,&|s_{i-1}|<|x_i|\end{cases} +|c_{i-1}|+|a_i|.$$

new.claim: The displayed quadratic form proves positive definiteness. The first pivot is $1$, $\widehat l_{21}=(1/2)/1=1/2$, and the second pivot is $1-(1/2)^2=3/4$ exactly, so the procedure succeeds through the square-root step.

old.quote: Input a Hermitian positive-definite matrix $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, whose real and imaginary components are in the floating-point system, in the convention of [[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]]; real matrices are included. Set L-hat=0. For j=1,...,n, form the diagonal sum from rounded real squares of the real and imaginary components of l_jk and rounded additions, then p_j=fl(a_jj-sum_{k<j}|l_jk|^2). If an operation fails or p_j is not positive normal, return failure(j). Set l_jj=fl(sqrt(p_j)); unless this is positive normal return failure(j). For i>j, form c_ij by sequential complex products with six real operations each and componentwise rounded additions; form r_ij=fl(a_ij-c_ij) componentwise and divide each real component by positive l_jj with one rounded real division. Any range failure returns failure(j) with the operation index. If all columns finish, return success(L-hat). The loops are finite. By [[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]], exact positive definiteness ensures an exact factor exists, but does not ensure the rounded algorithm succeeds.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A=A^*$ be positive definite in $\mathbb C^{n\times n}$. Suppose the rounded Cholesky algorithm succeeds with $\widehat L$. Put $m=20n+20$ and $g=\gamma_m=\frac{m u}{1-m u}$; assume $m u<1/5$. For $E=\widehat L\widehat L^*-A$, which is Hermitian, and with $|M|$ denoting entrywise absolute value for matrices,
$$|E|\le100g\,|\widehat L|\,|\widehat L|^*\quad\hbox{entrywise},\qquad \|E\|_F\le100g\|\widehat L\|_F^2,\qquad \|E\|_2\le100g\|\widehat L\|_F^2.$$
Thus $c_n(u)u=\frac{100m u}{1-m u}$. If also $100\sqrt n\,g\le1/2$, then
$$\|E\|_F\le200\sqrt n\,g\|A\|_F,\qquad \|E\|_2\le200\sqrt n\,g\|A\|_F.$$
These bounds apply on success only; positive definiteness does not guarantee rounded success.

Input a Hermitian positive-definite matrix $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, whose real and imaginary components are in the floating-point system, using the convention of [[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]]; real matrices are included. Initialize every entry of $\widehat L$ to zero. Process columns $j=1,\ldots,n$ in increasing order. For the diagonal, initialize $s=0$ and, for $k=1,\ldots,j-1$ in increasing order, compute
$$r_k=\operatorname{fl}(\Re(\widehat l_{jk})^2),\quad t_k=\operatorname{fl}(\Im(\widehat l_{jk})^2),\quad q_k=\operatorname{fl}(r_k+t_k),\quad s=\operatorname{fl}(s+q_k),$$
in that order. Then compute $p_j=\operatorname{fl}(a_{jj}-s)$. If an operation fails, or if $p_j$ is not positive and normal, return `failure` with pivot $j$ and the first failing operation location. Otherwise compute $\widehat l_{jj}=\operatorname{fl}(\sqrt{p_j})$; if it is not positive and normal, return `failure` at pivot $j$.

For each $i=j+1,\ldots,n$ in increasing order, initialize the complex accumulator $c_{ij}=0$. For $k=1,\ldots,j-1$ in increasing order, compute the complex product $w_{ik}=\widehat l_{ik}\overline{\widehat l_{jk}}$ using exactly the six real operations of the complex-product convention in [[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]], then update
$$\Re(c_{ij})\gets\operatorname{fl}(\Re(c_{ij})+\Re(w_{ik})),\qquad \Im(c_{ij})\gets\operatorname{fl}(\Im(c_{ij})+\Im(w_{ik})).$$
After this dot product, compute $r_{ij}=a_{ij}-c_{ij}$ by one rounded real subtraction for each component, then compute each component of $\widehat l_{ij}=r_{ij}/\widehat l_{jj}$ by one rounded real division. The empty dot product is zero. On any failure return `failure` with pivot $j$ and its first failing operation location (stage, column, row, inner index, component, and operation where applicable), with the diagonal and row loops ordered as stated. If all columns finish, return `success(\widehat L)`. All loops are finite. By [[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]], exact positive definiteness ensures an exact factor exists, but does not ensure the rounded algorithm succeeds.

new.claim: The spacing above $1$ is $2^{-52}$, so $1+2^{-53}$ is the midpoint between $1$ and $1+2^{-52}$. The even-significand endpoint is $1$; hence $s=1$. The next exact operands give $z=1-1=0$, $v=1-0=1$, $w=1-1=0$, and $t=2^{-53}-0=2^{-53}$. Each is representable, so each subtraction is exact.

The final exact intermediate is $w+t=2^{-53}$, hence $e=2^{-53}$. The first exact sum $1+2^{-53}$ and every later nonzero exact intermediate ($1$ or $2^{-53}$) are normal and within range; the zero intermediates are allowed by [F3]. Thus the call succeeds, its format satisfies [F2], and $s+e=1+2^{-53}=a+b$ exactly, also directly verified by these outputs.
The determinant is 2^-27, while direct multiplication gives (A^T A)_22=1+2^-54.
Since 2^-54<2^-53, the exact entry is strictly below the RNE midpoint above 1 and rounds to 1. The rounded Gram matrix has equal rows and is singular.
The exact result [F1] acts on the full-rank A without a Gram formation. The computed conclusion [F2] applies only if its separate successful-step hypotheses hold.
Direct multiplication by A^-1=diag(1,2^40) gives x=A^-1b=(1,0)^T and x-tilde=A^-1b-tilde=(1,1)^T; uniqueness follows from [F1].
The input difference and x norm are both measured against unit vectors: ||b-tilde-b||_2/||b||_2=2^-40 and ||x-tilde-x||_2/||x||_2=1.

For every $z$, $\|Az\|_2^2=z_1^2+2^{-80}z_2^2\le\|z\|_2^2$, with equality at $e_1$, so [F4] gives $\|A\|_2=1$. Likewise $\|A^{-1}z\|_2^2=z_1^2+2^{80}z_2^2\le2^{80}\|z\|_2^2$, with equality at $e_2$, hence $\|A^{-1}\|_2=2^{40}$. Thus [F3] gives $\kappa_2(A)=2^{40}$. The exact data calculation proves order-one forward change under a relative $2^{-40}$ right-hand-side perturbation; backward stability [F2] alone is not a forward-accuracy guarantee.

old.claim:
By [L1], $-|x|\le x\le|x|$ and $-|y|\le y\le|y|$. Adding gives
$-(|x|+|y|)\le x+y\le|x|+|y|$, hence $|x+y|\le|x|+|y|$. The product
identity follows by considering the four sign choices for $x$ and $y$ in the
piecewise definition [L1].

For $z=x+iy$ and $w=u+iv$, expansion gives
$$
|zw|^2=(xu-yv)^2+(xv+yu)^2=(x^2+y^2)(u^2+v^2)=|z|^2|w|^2.
$$
Both moduli are nonnegative by [L2], so uniqueness of nonnegative square
roots [L3] gives $|zw|=|z||w|$.

The identity
$$
(x^2+y^2)(u^2+v^2)-(xu+yv)^2=(xv-yu)^2\ge0.
$$
Thus $(xu+yv)^2\le|z|^2|w|^2$. Taking nonnegative square roots gives
$|xu+yv|\le|z||w|$, hence $xu+yv\le|z||w|$.
Thus $|z+w|^2=|z|^2+|w|^2+2(xu+yv)\le(|z|+|w|)^2$; nonnegative square roots give
$|z+w|\le|z|+|w|$. By the reciprocal formula in [L2],
$w(1/w)=(u+iv)(u-iv)/(u^2+v^2)=1$. Step 1.2 gives
$|w||1/w|=|1|=1$. Here $|w|>0$: otherwise $x^2+y^2=0$ forces $x=y=0$
because each square is nonnegative, contrary to $w\ne0$. Hence
$|1/w|=1/|w|$, and another application of step 1.2 yields
$|z/w|=|z|/|w|$.

old.claim:
For $x>0$, the initial lower candidate is $0$ and its square is at most
$x$. The initial upper candidate is $2^{n+1}\delta=2^{m+1}$; if $j=2m$ its
square is $2^{j+2}>x$, and if $j=2m+1$ its square is $2^{j+1}>x$. Thus initially
$(L\delta)^2\le x<(U\delta)^2$.

At each iteration, $Q$ lies strictly between the integer endpoints. The
exact comparison sets $L=Q$ only when $(Q\delta)^2\le x$, preserving the left
inequality; otherwise it sets $U=Q$, preserving the strict right inequality.
The square function is strictly increasing on nonnegative reals by [L3], so
the invariant implies $L\delta\le\sqrt{x}<U\delta$. The integer gap is
halved until it equals one;
the returned width is then $\delta$.

For $x=0$ the returned point interval is exact. For $x>0$, outward storage
rounding preserves both inequalities by [L2], so the stored result still
contains $\sqrt{x}$.

On a fixed exponent bin, step 1.2 gives endpoints
$\delta\lfloor\sqrt{x}/\delta\rfloor$ and
$\delta(\lfloor\sqrt{x}/\delta\rfloor+1)$, both nondecreasing in $x$. At
the transition from exponent $2m$ to $2m+1$, $\delta$ is unchanged. At the
transition from exponent $2m+1$ to $2m+2$, the square-root threshold is
$2^{m+1}$ and the grid spacing doubles from $\delta$ to $2\delta$. Just below
the threshold the lower and upper endpoints are at most $2^{m+1}$; at or
above it they are at least $2^{m+1}$. Thus both exact endpoint functions are
nondecreasing across each transition. At $x=0$ both are zero. The directed
rounding maps are nondecreasing by their greatest-lower/least-upper
definitions, so storage preserves this order.

If $a=b$, the singleton range consists only of $f(a)$, so the conclusion

subcollection covers; taking its largest index shows $|f|$ is bounded.

old.claim:
For real addition and subtraction, every exact pair value lies between the
endpoint formulas. For multiplication, fixing one variable makes the product
affine in the other, so a minimum or maximum over a rectangle is attained at a
corner. Reciprocal is monotone on either interval avoiding zero, and square
root is monotone on $[0,\infty)$. Thus the exact ranges lie in the displayed
pre-rounding intervals. Each computed lower endpoint is no greater than the
exact lower endpoint and each upper endpoint is no smaller than the exact
upper endpoint by [L2]; square-root endpoint bounds follow from [L3]. For
complex rectangles, component addition and multiplication preserve the exact
component formulas. If a rectangle excludes zero, at least one coordinate
interval omits zero, so its squared interval has positive lower endpoint;
component interval operations then enclose the exact reciprocal and quotient.

For a ball $B(c,r)$, the coordinate projection intervals in [L1] contain
each real and imaginary component. Since
$(|\Re z|+|\Im z|)^2\ge(\Re z)^2+(\Im z)^2$, [L3] gives
$|z|\le|\Re z|+|\Im z|\le M_B$. Also
$|z|\ge|\Re z|\ge d(X_B)$ and $|z|\ge|\Im z|\ge d(Y_B)$ by [L2]–[L3], so

$m_{B_2}>0$, then $|w|\ge m_{B_2}$ and

bounds, proving soundness of all finite ball results.

interval. Therefore $M_B$ cannot decrease and $m_B$ cannot increase as an
input ball enlarges. The ball addition, subtraction and multiplication
radii in [L1] are consequently nondecreasing. If both divisor results are
finite, the larger divisor ball has positive $m_B$ and the smaller one has at
least as large an $m_B$; the quotient radius therefore cannot decrease when
either ball is enlarged. For intervals and rectangles, the exact endpoint
hulls and their downward/upward roundings preserve inclusion, so their finite
extensions are isotone as well; for square root, [L3] gives monotonicity of
the computed endpoint maps. If a domain restriction is lost, the
operation returns its stated non-finite status.

In any nonempty finite acyclic graph, some node has no predecessor:
otherwise, repeatedly following predecessors would revisit a node by
finiteness and create a directed cycle. Remove such a node and repeat to
construct a finite topological order. By [L1], input nodes contain their
assigned values and constants have certified enclosures. Induct along this
order: if each predecessor of an operation node contains its exact value,
steps 1.1–1.3 show that the operation enclosure contains the node's exact
value. The induction covers every node, including the root, for every
admissible assignment.

in the format of
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. If either exact

$[\min(ac,ad,bc,bd),\max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]$. Division is defined only when
$0\notin Y$ and is $X[1/d,1/c]$, with reciprocal endpoints computed as exact
rationals before outward rounding. Squaring is
$[0,\max(a^2,b^2)]$ when $0\in X$ and
$[\min(a^2,b^2),\max(a^2,b^2)]$ otherwise. Square root is defined only for
$X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and is enclosed by applying
[[alg-dyadic-square-root-bisection]] to the exact dyadic endpoints with
request $n=p$, where $p$ is the selected format precision, and rounding
outward for storage.

If $0\in Y$ for division, return `split-domain` with the two subdomains
$Y\cap(-\infty,0)$ and $Y\cap(0,\infty)$, or `entire` when the caller does not
request subdivision. No finite quotient interval is returned in this case.
An invalid square-root domain returns `domain-error` or an explicitly
restricted nonnegative subdomain.

Complex-rectangle addition, subtraction and multiplication use
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$, applying the real interval operations to
each component. For a rectangle $X+iY$ excluding $0$, define its reciprocal by
$(X-iY)/(X^2+Y^2)$; the denominator interval is strictly positive because at
least one coordinate interval excludes zero. Division multiplies by this
reciprocal.

For a ball $B(c,r)$, let $X_B=[\Re c-r,\Re c+r]$ and
$Y_B=[\Im c-r,\Im c+r]$ be its coordinate projection intervals. For a real
interval $J$, let $M(J)=\max(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$ and let $d(J)=0$ if
$0\in J$, otherwise $d(J)=\min(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$. Put

$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}+M_{B_2}))$, multiplication as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}M_{B_2}))$, and division as

origin-centered output balls are conservative but inclusion-isotone. If

On each bounded square, the factorial series and their tails converge
uniformly by [L8]. Their Cauchy products are absolutely convergent and can be
grouped by total degree by [L9]. For sine, the coefficient of $x^r y^s$
in $\sin(x+y)$ vanishes when $r+s$ is even and otherwise equals
$(-1)^{(r+s-1)/2}/(r!s!)$, by the binomial theorem; the same coefficient
appears in $\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y$. For cosine, the coefficient in
$\cos(x+y)$ vanishes when $r+s$ is odd and otherwise equals
$(-1)^{(r+s)/2}/(r!s!)$, matching $\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y$. Thus both
addition identities hold.

On every bounded interval, [L8] gives absolute convergence of the
factorial coefficient series and their derivative series. Applying [L5] to the
two power series gives $\sin'=\cos$ and $\cos'=-\sin$. By the product rule
in [L4], the derivative of $\sin^2x+\cos^2x$ is zero; [L3] and its value
$1$ at zero give $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$.

old.quote:
Every integral below is the oriented Riemann integral constructed from upper
and lower Darboux sums in
[[lem-continuous-functions-riemann-integrable]]. It exists for each displayed
continuous integrand on the finite interval between its endpoints, is additive
in intervals, reverses sign when the endpoints are reversed, is monotone in
the integrand, and satisfies
$|\int_a^b g(t)\,dt|\le|b-a|\max_{t\text{ between }a\text{ and }b}|g(t)|$.
These properties also
give constant comparison bounds and the average-value difference quotient
used to differentiate the integral-defined functions.

The exponential is $\exp(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}x^k/k!$ for $x\in\mathbb R$.
The sine and cosine are the everywhere-convergent power series
$\sin x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k+1}/(2k+1)!$ and
$\cos x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k}/(2k)!$. Define
$\arctan x=\int_0^x dt/(1+t^2)$ and set $\pi=4\arctan1$. The natural
logarithm $\ln$ is defined on $(0,\infty)$ by $\ln x=\int_1^x dt/t$.

The square root is the unique nonnegative real $y$ with $y^2=x$ for $x\ge0$;
existence and uniqueness follow from
[[lem-nonnegative-square-root-exists-and-unique]]. The tangent is
$\tan x=\sin x/\cos x$ on the set where $\cos x\ne0$.

For complex $z=x+iy$, the modulus $|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ is defined in
[[def-intervals-rectangles-and-complex-balls]]. The complex exponential is
$\exp(x+iy)=\exp(x)(\cos y+i\sin y)$. The principal complex logarithm is
$\operatorname{Log}(z)=\ln|z|+i\operatorname{Arg}(z)$ on
$\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$. For $z=x+iy$ in this domain, define
$$
\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)=
\begin{cases}
\arctan(y/x),&x>0,\\
\pi/2,&x=0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi/2,&x=0,\ y<0,\\
\pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0.
\end{cases}
$$
The excluded negative real axis is the remaining case $x<0,y=0$; zero is
also excluded.

These are point functions. An interval extension must separately enclose their
exact ranges, test the stated domains, and return a non-finite status when its
finite budget cannot certify a reduction or endpoint.

For $|u|\le1/2$ and integer $N\ge1$, set
$E_N(u)=\sum_{k=0}^N u^k/k!$ and
$R_E=|u|^{N+1}/((N+1)!(1-|u|/(N+2)))$. Then
$\exp(u)\in[E_N(u)-R_E,E_N(u)+R_E]$, and the lower endpoint is positive.
For $y\in[1,2]$, put $v=(y-1)/(y+1)$ and
$L_N(v)=2\sum_{k=0}^N v^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$. Then
$$
\left|\ln y-L_N(v)\right|\le
\frac{2|v|^{2N+3}}{(2N+3)(1-v^2)}.
$$
For every integer $j$ and $y>0$, the natural logarithm also satisfies
$\ln(2^j y)=j\ln2+\ln y$.
For $|t|\le1/2$, set $A_N(t)=\sum_{k=0}^N(-1)^kt^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$. Then
$$
\left|\arctan t-A_N(t)\right|\le
\frac{|t|^{2N+3}}{(2N+3)(1-t^2)}.
$$

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on
$(a,b)$, with $a<b$. Then there is $c\in(a,b)$ such that
$$
f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a).
$$

Every function differentiable at $c$ is continuous at $c$.
If $f,g$ are real functions differentiable at $c$, then $f+g$ and $fg$ are
differentiable there and
$$
(f+g)'(c)=f'(c)+g'(c),\qquad (fg)'(c)=f'(c)g(c)+f(c)g'(c).
$$
If $g(c)\ne0$, then $f/g$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$$
(f/g)'(c)=\frac{f'(c)g(c)-f(c)g'(c)}{g(c)^2}.
$$
If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, $g$ is differentiable at $f(c)$, and the
composition is defined near $c$, then $g\circ f$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$(g\circ f)'(c)=g'(f(c))f'(c)$. For every integer $m\ge1$,
$(x^m)'=mx^{m-1}$.

Let $R_0>0$ and let $(a_n)_{n\ge0}$ be real coefficients such that for every
$0<R<R_0$ both $\sum_{n\ge0}|a_n|R^n$ and
$\sum_{n\ge1}n|a_n|R^{n-1}$ converge. Then
$F(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n$ is differentiable for $|x|<R_0$, with
$F'(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}na_nx^{n-1}$.
In a Dedekind-complete ordered field, the natural numbers are unbounded above.

For real $x,y$, $|xy|=|x||y|$ and $|x+y|\le|x|+|y|$. For complex
$z,w$, $|zw|=|z||w|$, $|z+w|\le|z|+|w|$, and if $w\ne0$ then
$|z/w|=|z|/|w|$.

For every real $R\ge0$, the factorial series
$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}R^n/n!$ converges. If $N\ge0$ and
$q=R/(N+2)<1$, its tail after index $N$ satisfies
$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}\frac{R^n}{n!}
\le \frac{R^{N+1}}{(N+1)!(1-q)}.
$$
Consequently the series defining $\exp x$, $\sin x$, $\cos x$ and each of
their formal derivative series converge absolutely and uniformly on every
bounded interval $|x|\le R$. For $0\le r<1$, the geometric series and the
odd power series $\sum_{k\ge0}x^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$, with their formal derivative
series, converge absolutely and uniformly on $|x|\le r$.

Let $\sum_{n\ge0}a_n=A$ and $\sum_{n\ge0}b_n=B$ be absolutely convergent
real series. Define
$$
c_n=\sum_{j=0}^n a_jb_{n-j}.
$$
Then $\sum_{n\ge0}c_n$ converges absolutely and has sum $AB$. Thus the
product of the two series can be grouped by total degree without changing
its sum.

old.claim:
For an exponential input interval, the fixed scale puts every scaled point
in $[-1/2,1/2]$. The point bound [L3] with $|u|$ replaced by the interval's
largest absolute endpoint gives a uniform tail enclosure. The truncated
polynomial interval-evaluates every point by [L2]. The tail radius increases
with the largest absolute input, and each repeated interval square preserves
inclusion by [L2]. The exact identity
$\exp(x)=(\exp(x/2^s))^{2^s}$ follows by multiplying the absolutely
convergent series $2^s$ times: the multinomial theorem gives coefficient
$(2^s)^k/k!$ at degree $k$; each squaring
preserves the enclosure by [L2].

On each positive logarithm bin, every $y$ maps to
$v=(y-1)/(y+1)\in[0,1/3]$. The interval series and uniform tail from [L3]
contain $\ln y$; [L3] also proves the exact logarithm scaling identity used by
the algorithm. Each interval transform and sum preserves inclusion by [L2].
The fixed bin partition ensures that enlarging the input only enlarges the
intersection with each bin, so its interval-series enclosure and the final
hull also enlarge. The arctangent transformations follow from [L5]; on each
fixed branch the rational interval maps and fixed series are isotone, and the
tail radius is nondecreasing in the largest absolute transformed endpoint.

The outward cell interval built from $P_N$ contains each exact canonical
cell, since $\pi\in P_N$; thus its intersection hull $X_k$ contains every
input point assigned to that cell, and $X_k-kP_N/2$ contains the exact
residual $r=x-k\pi/2$. The algorithm certifies this residual inside the
Taylor range. By [L4], exact sine and cosine values are the stated signed
swaps of $\sin r$ and $\cos r$. The polynomial interval
evaluation contains each truncated value by [L2], and adding the symmetric
tail interval from [L4] contains the omitted remainder. Taking the hull over
all intersected cells therefore contains the full range. If the interval
width is at least $2\pi$, [L4] gives the safe range $[-1,1]$. For nested
inputs, each fixed canonical cell intersection enlarges and its fixed-term
interval evaluation is isotone by [L2]; the hull is therefore nested on the reduced branch. Exact rational interval
polynomial and tail operations are inclusion-isotone, and the final directed
endpoint conversions are nondecreasing. Intersecting with $[-1,1]$ preserves
containment and nesting, and ensures that the wide-input $[-1,1]$ return
contains every narrower finite result.

Tangent is defined only where cosine is nonzero. On a piece whose cosine
enclosure excludes zero, division is sound by [L2] and contains every
$\sin x/\cos x$. If cosine may vanish, the algorithm returns a split or
non-finite status, so no unsound finite value is reported. The same argument
applies to square root using the bisection supplier in [L2].

Evaluate the finite expression DAG in topological order. Every primitive
node encloses its exact value by steps 1.1–2.2; induction over the finite
node order then encloses every exact intermediate and the root range. Each
primitive's canonical partition and fixed truncation are nested on common
finite branches, so the same induction preserves inclusion for nested inputs.

applications of [L6] to the absolutely convergent series for $\exp u$ show
that the coefficient of $u^k$ in $(\exp u)^d$ is
$$
\sum_{n_1+\cdots+n_d=k}\frac1{n_1!\cdots n_d!}
=\frac{d^k}{k!},
$$
where the equality is the multinomial theorem. Thus $(\exp u)^d=\exp(du)$;
set $u=x/d$. Each interval squaring preserves the resulting enclosure by
[L2].

On each positive logarithm bin, every $y$ maps to
$v=(y-1)/(y+1)\in[0,1/3]$. The interval series and uniform tail from [L3]
contain $\ln y$; [L3] also proves the exact logarithm scaling identity used by
the algorithm. Each interval transform and sum preserves inclusion by [L2].
The fixed bin partition ensures that enlarging the input only enlarges the
intersection with each bin, so its interval-series enclosure and the final
hull also enlarge. The arctangent transformations follow from [L5]; on each
fixed branch the rational interval maps and fixed series are isotone, and the
tail radius is nondecreasing in the largest absolute transformed endpoint.

The outward cell interval built from $P_N$ contains each exact canonical
cell, since $\pi\in P_N$; thus its intersection hull $X_k$ contains every
input point assigned to that cell, and $X_k-kP_N/2$ contains the exact
residual $r=x-k\pi/2$. The algorithm certifies this residual inside the
Taylor range. By [L4], exact sine and cosine values are the stated signed
swaps of $\sin r$ and $\cos r$. The polynomial interval
evaluation contains each truncated value by [L2], and adding the symmetric
tail interval from [L4] contains the omitted remainder. Taking the hull over
all intersected cells therefore contains the full range. If the interval
width is at least $2\pi$, [L4] gives the safe range $[-1,1]$. For nested
inputs, each fixed canonical cell intersection enlarges and its fixed-term
interval evaluation is isotone by [L2]; the hull is therefore nested on the reduced branch. Exact rational interval
polynomial and tail operations are inclusion-isotone, and the final directed
endpoint conversions are nondecreasing. Intersecting with $[-1,1]$ preserves
containment and nesting, and ensures that the wide-input $[-1,1]$ return
contains every narrower finite result.

Tangent is defined only where cosine is nonzero. On a piece whose cosine
enclosure excludes zero, division is sound by [L2] and contains every
$\sin x/\cos x$. If cosine may vanish, the algorithm returns a split or
non-finite status, so no unsound finite value is reported. The same argument
applies to square root using the bisection supplier in [L2].

Evaluate the finite expression DAG in topological order. Every primitive
node encloses its exact value by steps 1.1–2.2; induction over the finite
node order then encloses every exact intermediate and every requested output
range. Each primitive's canonical partition and fixed truncation are nested
on common finite branches, so the same induction preserves inclusion for
nested inputs evaluated with the same format and truncation index.

Input: a finite expression DAG with real interval or complex rectangle input,
a finite dyadic format and an integer truncation index $N\ge1$. All constants,
including the Machin enclosure of $\pi$, use the same fixed $N$ and format
throughout a call. Output: a finite interval/rectangle enclosure, or one of
`empty`, `domain-error`, `split-domain`, `overflow`, or `inconclusive` with the
unresolved domain piece. No value from a system `libm` routine is treated as a
certified endpoint.

1. Evaluate arithmetic nodes by
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]. On an invalid divisor
return its declared status. For $\sqrt{X}$ require $X\subseteq[0,\infty)$; for
$\ln X$ require $X\subseteq(0,\infty)$. If an input is not wholly in the
stated domain, return `domain-error` rather than silently discarding points.

2. Set $s=\max(0,e_{\max}+2)$, using the exponent in
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. Since
$N_{\max}<2^{e_{\max}+1}$, exact dyadic comparison gives
$N_{\max}/2^s<1/2$. For an
interval $X$, evaluate the truncated exponential polynomial on $U=X/2^s$ by
interval arithmetic, add the symmetric tail using $\max_{u\in U}|u|$, then
square the resulting interval $s$ times. If its lower endpoint is not
positive or an endpoint overflows, return `inconclusive` or `overflow`. For
$\ln$, split $X\subset(0,\infty)$ into its intersections with the fixed
dyadic bins $[2^j,2^{j+1}]$. On each nonempty piece set
$Y=2^{-j}X_j\subseteq[1,2]$, $V=(Y-1)/(Y+1)$, evaluate the positive logarithm
series on $V$ with its tail determined by $\max|V|$, and combine
$j\ln2+\ln Y$ by outward arithmetic. Take the hull over all intersected
bins.

3. Partition $\arctan$ input at the fixed real breakpoints
$-3,-1/2,1/2,3$. On pieces within $[-1/2,1/2]$, use its alternating power
series interval evaluation. For $t\in[1/2,1]$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/4-\arctan((1-t)/(1+t))$; for $t\in[1,3]$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/4+\arctan((t-1)/(t+1))$; for $t>3$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/2-\arctan(1/t)$. Use odd symmetry on negative pieces.
Enclose $\pi$ by Machin's identity and the alternating series at $1/5$ and
$1/239$, forming their rational partial sums and tail endpoints exactly
before the final outward conversion. If any branch test is unresolved, return
`inconclusive`.

4. For sine and cosine, first compute one outward Machin interval $P_N$ for
$\pi$ using the same $N$ and format, with the rational series endpoints
combined exactly before final outward conversion. If $P_N$ is non-finite or
its lower endpoint is not positive, return `inconclusive`. For finite input
$X=[a,b]$, put $M_X=\max(|a|,|b|)$, $p_-:=\inf(P_N)>0$, and

$-(2|k|-1)p_-/4<-M_X$. Thus every cell enclosure that can intersect $X$ is

its intersection with $X$; do not round candidate-cell or residual endpoints.
Include every cell whose $P_N$ enclosure cannot be ruled out as intersecting
$X$. Certify the residual enclosure $R=X_k-kP_N/2$ satisfies
$R\subseteq[-1,1]$, evaluate the corresponding power
polynomial and add the explicit geometric tail by exact rational interval
arithmetic, then round the final endpoints outward. The tail comes from
[[lem-trigonometric-identities-machin-and-range-reduction]], and map by the
quarter-period identities. Intersect every finite sine/cosine enclosure
with $[-1,1]$, including after the sign and coordinate swaps; the exact
values satisfy these bounds. If the input width is at least $2\sup(P_N)$,
return $[-1,1]$. If a cell cannot be certified in the reduced interval or the
finite candidate list cannot be resolved, return `inconclusive`. For tangent,
divide the sine enclosure by the cosine enclosure only on canonical pieces
where the latter excludes zero; otherwise return `split-domain` or
`inconclusive`.

$\sin(Y)$ and combine them by rectangle operations. For principal
$\operatorname{Log}$, require a rectangle excluding zero and every point of
the negative real branch cut; otherwise return `domain-error`. Subdivide into
sign-stable quadrants and axis pieces; on the quadrants use
$$
\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)=
\begin{cases}
\arctan(y/x),&x>0,\ y>0,\\
-\arctan((-y)/x),&x>0,\ y<0,\\
\pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0.
\end{cases}
$$
For $x=0,y>0$ set $\operatorname{Arg}(iy)=\pi/2$, for $x=0,y<0$ set it to

in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain

node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

$$

$$

$$

$$

Input: a finite, well-formed, typed expression DAG with one or more designated
output nodes; finite real interval or complex rectangle assignments for its
input nodes; exact dyadic constants or constants supplied with certified
enclosing intervals/rectangles; a finite dyadic format $(p,e_{\min},e_{\max})$
with $p\ge2$ and $e_{\min}\le e_{\max}$; and an integer truncation index
$N\ge1$. Input interval endpoints and supplied constant enclosures use this
format. All constants, including every Machin enclosure of $\pi$, use the
same fixed $N$ and format throughout a call. Real nodes support input and
constant nodes and the operations $+,-,\times,\div,\sqrt{\phantom{x}},
\exp,\ln,\arctan,\sin,\cos,\tan$. Complex nodes support input and constant
nodes and $+,-,\times,\div,\exp,\operatorname{Log}$. Each operation has
homogeneous real or complex inputs of its stated type; no implicit conversion
between real and complex nodes is performed. Unsupported node types, arities,
or type combinations return `inconclusive` with the offending node.

Output: a finite interval/rectangle enclosure for every designated output
node, or one of `empty`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `split-domain`, `overflow`,
or `inconclusive` with the node and unresolved domain piece. If any supplied
input is `empty`, return `empty`. No value from a system `libm` routine is
treated as a certified endpoint. Each DAG node is evaluated once; shared nodes
reuse their interval/rectangle enclosure and do not preserve correlations
between distinct paths.

1. Check that node identifiers are unique, all references resolve, every
designated output is a node, and the supported node types and arities above
hold. Use each supplied input enclosure as its node value. For an exact real
dyadic constant $c$, use $[\operatorname{rd}(c),\operatorname{ru}(c)]$ in the
selected format. For an exact complex dyadic constant, do this to each
coordinate. A finite subnormal endpoint remains a valid endpoint; if a
coordinate conversion overflows, return `overflow` with that constant node.
Use a supplied certified constant enclosure as given. Construct a topological
order by repeatedly removing a node whose
predecessors have already been removed, breaking ties by lexicographically
smallest node identifier. If no such node exists before all nodes are ordered,
return `inconclusive` with a node in the cycle. Evaluate nodes in this order
and store each finite enclosure for its successors. Arithmetic nodes use
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]; if an operation returns
a non-finite status, propagate it immediately with its node and unresolved
piece. For $\sqrt{X}$ require $X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and for $\ln X$ require
$X\subseteq(0,\infty)$; otherwise return `domain-error` rather than silently
discarding points.

2. For a real exponential node, set $s=\max(0,e_{\max}+2)$ using the format
in [[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. Since
$N_{\max}<2^{e_{\max}+1}$, exact comparison gives $N_{\max}/2^s<1/2$. For
its input interval $X$, evaluate the degree-$N$ exponential polynomial on
$U=X/2^s$ by interval arithmetic and add the symmetric tail from
[[lem-range-reduced-exp-log-and-arctan-series-enclosures]], using
$\max_{u\in U}|u|$. Square the resulting interval $s$ times. If its lower
endpoint is not positive or an endpoint overflows, return `inconclusive` or
`overflow` with the node and input interval.

For a real logarithm node, first require $X\subseteq(0,\infty)$. List all
integers $j$ for which $X_j=X\cap[2^j,2^{j+1}]$ is nonempty; exact endpoint
comparisons find this finite list because $X$ has positive finite endpoints.
On each piece set $Y=2^{-j}X_j\subseteq[1,2]$ and $V=(Y-1)/(Y+1)$, evaluate
the positive logarithm series on $V$ with its tail determined by $\max|V|$,
and form $j\ln2+\ln Y$ by outward arithmetic. Compute the fixed enclosure for
$\ln2$ once by the same series and tail at $y=2$, hence $v=1/3$, and reuse it
in every bin. If any piece cannot be evaluated finitely, propagate its status
and that piece. Otherwise take the interval hull of all piece enclosures as
the node enclosure.

3. Partition a real arctangent input at the fixed breakpoints
$-3,-1/2,1/2,3$ into nonempty closed pieces, allowing shared endpoints.
On pieces in $[-1/2,1/2]$, evaluate its alternating power series. For positive
pieces in $[1/2,1]$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/4-\arctan((1-t)/(1+t))$; in $[1,3]$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/4+\arctan((t-1)/(t+1))$; for $t>3$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/2-\arctan(1/t)$. Evaluate negative pieces by odd symmetry.
Enclose $\pi$ using Machin's identity and the alternating series at $1/5$ and
$1/239$, forming rational partial sums and tail endpoints exactly before
final outward conversion. If every piece is finite, take the interval hull of
all piece enclosures. If any branch test or piece is unresolved, return its
non-finite status with that piece and do not use a partial hull.

4. For each sine or cosine node, first compute one outward Machin interval
$P_N$ for $\pi$ using the same $N$ and format, combining the rational series
endpoints exactly before final outward conversion. If $P_N$ is non-finite or
its lower endpoint is not positive, return `inconclusive`. For finite input
$X=[a,b]$, put $M_X=\max(|a|,|b|)$, $p_-:=\inf(P_N)>0$, and
$K=\lceil2M_X/p_-\rceil+1$, with the ceiling computed by exact rational
comparisons. If the width of $X$ is at least $2\sup(P_N)$, return

the canonical cells $[k\pi/2-\pi/4,k\pi/2+\pi/4]$. For each candidate form
the exact rational interval enclosure
$C_k=kP_N/2+[-1/4,1/4]P_N$ of its canonical cell. For $k>K$, the exact
left endpoint $(2k-1)\pi/4$ of cell $k$ is at least
$(2k-1)p_-/4>M_X$; for $k<-K$, its exact right endpoint
$-(2|k|-1)\pi/4$ is at most $-(2|k|-1)p_-/4<-M_X$. Thus no omitted exact
cell can intersect $X$. Include each candidate whose $C_k$ intersects $X$;
exclude only candidates whose intersection is empty by exact comparison. Let

endpoints, and form the residual enclosure $R_k=X_k-kP_N/2$. Certify

geometric tail from [[lem-trigonometric-identities-machin-and-range-reduction]]
by exact rational interval arithmetic. Map each enclosure by the appropriate
quarter-period sign or coordinate swap and intersect it with $[-1,1]$.

If no candidate is included, a cell cannot be certified in the reduced
interval, or any candidate endpoint overflows, return `inconclusive` or
`overflow` with the cell; never omit that piece from a finite hull.

cosine. Divide the sine enclosure by the cosine enclosure only when the latter
excludes zero. If a piece contains a certified cosine zero, return

certified, return `inconclusive`. Take the interval hull of tangent enclosures
only when every piece is finite.

and $\sin(Y)$ and combine their enclosures by rectangle operations. For
principal $\operatorname{Log}$, first require a rectangle excluding zero and
every point of the negative real branch cut; otherwise return `domain-error`.
Compute an outward Machin interval $P_N$ for $\pi$ using this call's $N$ and
format; if it is non-finite or its lower endpoint is not positive, return
`inconclusive`.

strictly positive portions, plus the singleton $\{0\}$ when it contains zero.
Use the closures of the strictly signed portions as interval enclosures; form
their Cartesian products for the quadrant pieces, and handle products with an
axis singleton separately. Omit empty pieces. These finitely many pieces
cover the rectangle, with quadrant closures allowed to overlap their axis
pieces. On a quadrant where the denominator interval excludes zero, use
$$
\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)=
\begin{cases}
\arctan(y/x),&x>0,\ y>0,\\
-\arctan((-y)/x),&x>0,\ y<0,\\
\pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0.
\end{cases}
$$

$$

S_{\rm III}=[-p_+,-p_-/2],\qquad S_{\rm IV}=[-p_+/2,0].
$$

with the piece and status `empty-argument-intersection`; do not omit the
piece. If the denominator interval has a zero endpoint, use $J=S_q$
instead of a ratio formula.

conversion $H(J)=[\operatorname{rd}(a),\operatorname{ru}(b)]$ in the selected
format. Perform this conversion after intersection for a ratio branch and
after selecting $S_q$ for a coarse branch. Finite subnormal endpoints are
accepted; an overflow returns `overflow` with the piece. On the positive
imaginary axis use $H(P_N/2)$, on the negative imaginary axis use
$H(-P_N/2)$, and on the positive real axis use $H([0,0])$. The initial domain
check excludes the origin and negative real axis, so these are all remaining
axis cases.

On each piece enclose $\ln\sqrt{X^2+Y^2}$ using the real operations and
evaluator, and combine it with the converted argument interval into a
rectangle. If every piece is finite, take the coordinatewise hull of all
piece rectangles. If any piece, conversion or branch is unresolved, return
its status and piece without forming a partial hull.

terms; the exponential step performs exactly $s$ interval squarings. The

continuous integrand on the finite interval between its endpoints, is additive

old.claim:
There are at most $B$ splits. Each split adds one net box to the queue,
so at most $2B+1$ boxes are processed. Each leaf evaluation has a finite DAG,
uses at most $N+1$ terms per series, and has finitely many fixed domain bins or
quadrant pieces. Thus each evaluation and the whole queue procedure terminate.

The two halves at every split cover their parent by [L1]. Every completed
real or complex leaf enclosure contains its exact range by [L2] or [L3].
Induction upward through the finite split tree shows that the hull of all
completed leaf enclosures contains the range on the union of their boxes,
which is $X$.

The algorithm returns `certified` only after the queue is empty, every box
has a finite completed leaf, and the final hull satisfies the width test.
Otherwise it returns a non-finite status or `inconclusive`, retaining the
unresolved box or failed global-width result. Hence no failed branch or wide
hull is silently treated as tolerance success.

new.claim: The initial admission checks terminate: the format's subnormal index range, exponent range and significand ranges are finite, and each equality comparison of exact dyadics is decided by clearing powers of two and comparing integers. Their enumeration is exactly the selected representable set, so a passing endpoint test establishes membership, including for zero and subnormals. Invalid initial data stop before an evaluator call. For admitted data, every endpoint of the initial box belongs to that format. Inductively, a split enqueues children only after the exact midpoint passes the same membership test; all other endpoints are inherited from the parent. The DAG, output, constants, format and $N$ are unchanged. Hence every queued box satisfies the elementary evaluator's input conditions. Each such call terminates through its finite DAG, finite series, finite bisection and finite bin/cell/quadrant lists, or returns a specified failure. The membership guard also terminates and can stop immediately with `inconclusive`. There are at most $B$ admitted splits and therefore at most $2B+1$ processed boxes. Thus the entire procedure terminates, including every guard-stop branch.

Before a box is processed, the completed leaf boxes together with the queued boxes cover $X$. Removing a current box preserves this cover when that box is counted as the current unresolved parent. Completing it transfers it to the completed leaves; an admitted split replaces it by two closed children whose union is the parent by [L1]. A failed midpoint test retains the parent as unresolved and therefore discards no part of the cover. This proves the coverage invariant by induction. By step 1.1, each completed leaf was evaluated on admissible input, so its finite enclosure contains its exact range by [L2] or [L3]. If the queue empties without an early return, all covering leaves are completed; their enclosure hull therefore contains the exact range on all of $X$. On an early return, the completed-leaf hull is not asserted to cover the unresolved parent or remaining queue.

A `certified` return occurs only after the queue is empty without an admission, evaluator, split-guard or budget stop, and after the completed-leaf hull passes the final global width test. Step 2.1 then proves enclosure of the whole range, and the exact width comparison proves the requested tolerance. A failed midpoint membership instead returns `inconclusive` with the completed-leaf hull, unresolved parent, remaining queue and actual guard status; that partial hull is not a full-domain certificate. The other non-finite, exhausted-budget, unsplittable-coordinate and failed global-width branches likewise make no tolerance-success claim. Thus the finite guard preserves the stated certified-range, coverage and failure conclusions.
